sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
In recent years, extreme weather disasters have caused extremely adverse impacts
on the safe and stable operation of power systems. For example, in June 2020, Guangxi
in China faced strong wind challenges and more than 250,000 households experienced
power outages. More than 100 distribution lines at the 10-kV level were damaged [1]. In
February 2021, Texas in the United States suffered a snowstorm, with about five million
users experiencing power outages [2,3]. When extreme natural disasters occur, the failure
probability of power system components will increase significantly, which may cause cas-
cading power outages and bring serious impacts on social safety and energy supply [ 4].
Extreme weather disasters, as a type of low-frequency and high-impact events, not only
cause difficulties for power system operation and maintenance, but also result in large-scale
and long-term power outages, even causing continuous cascading failures. During the
disaster period, large-scale power outages will seriously affect the safe and stable operation
of power systems, threaten the reliability of power supply services, and have a great impact
on important social infrastructure. Therefore, whether the distribution network can ensure
and restore power supply to key loads after disasters has become an important research di-
rection at present [5]. At present, among various studies, hardening is a relatively common
Energies 2025, 18, 6353 https://doi.org/10.3390/en18236353
Energies 2025, 18, 6353 2 of 23
and effective measure to improve the physical resilience of the power system. Reference [6]
proposed a line hardening strategy to improve the physical resilience of distribution net-
works. However, this kind of model is usually strongly conservative and requires many
iterations, leading to long solving time. Reference [7] pointed out that hardening strategies
can affect the line failure probability but cannot reduce it to zero. Reference [8] considered
the uncertainty of photovoltaic output and improved the resilience of the distribution
network through the pre-deployment and dynamic scheduling of mobile energy storage.
Reference [9] focused on the resilience enhancement of distribution networks and proposed
a two-stage robust optimization scheme for line hardening and energy storage configu-
ration. Reference [10] established a distribution network resilience enhancement scheme
considering endogenous uncertainty by implementing pre-disaster line hardening and
real-time unit scheduling under typhoon disasters. Reference [11] studied the power–traffic
coupled system and enhanced the resilience of both the distribution and transportation
networks by expanding line and road capacities. However, the above studies adopted
full-level hardening measures and did not consider the impact of transportation network
resilience enhancement measures on post-disaster power system restoration.
Compared with full-level planning, differential planning improves the overall system
resilience in a targeted treatment manner [12]. By accurately allocating limited resources,
it realizes the coordinated optimization of disaster resistance capability and investment
effectiveness. Reference [13] considered line hardening and demand response mechanisms
in the gas–electric coupled distribution network and proposed a multi-level hardening
and resilience enhancement strategy for such systems. Reference [14] proposed multiple
performance evaluation indicators for transmission networks in typhoon-affected areas
and presented a differential hardening method for disaster-resistant backbone grids. Ref-
erence [15] considered the impact of extreme high-temperature weather on the new-type
power system and proposed a differential planning scheme based on a resilience evaluation
method considering load grading. Reference [16] considered load forecasting errors and
employed the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) and the deviation maximization method to
analyze the risk resistance capability of the distribution network
Uncertainty can be generally divided into two types: exogenous uncertainty and
endogenous uncertainty [17,18]. In exogenous uncertainty, the distribution of model pa-
rameters is known, for example, based on historical data or expert opinions Most existing
studies on uncertainty consider exogenous uncertainty, where decision variables have
no direct relationship with uncertainty. However, in fact, many problems are affected by
decisions, which is a kind of endogenous uncertainty, that is, decision-dependent uncer-
tainty (DDU) [18]. Reference [19] considers decision-dependent uncertainty and proposes
a novel multistage stochastic optimization model for network expansion planning. Since
extreme disasters are low-frequency and high-impact events for which historical probability
distributions may be sparse or unreliable, they need to be further addressed through ro-
bust optimization. Reference [20] considered the decision-dependent relationship between
investment portfolios in distribution systems and wildfire-induced line outages and pro-
posed a two-stage distributionally robust planning optimization problem. Reference [21]
considered strategic capacity withholding and decision dependence and developed a
market-oriented, risk-averse coordinated scheduling method. Reference [ 22] proposed
a new multi-stage stochastic scheduling model, considering DDU on the demand side.
Reference [23] proposed a robust dispatch strategy that accounts for the decision dependent
uncertainties arising from renewable energy sources and demand response. Reference [24]
studied the influence of DDU on vehicle ownership and charging behavior under incen-
tive policies. Reference [ 25] proposed a model considering multiple types of DDU and
introduced an improved algorithm to accelerate the solution process. Reference [ 26] con-
Energies 2025, 18, 6353 3 of 23
sidered the decision-dependent uncertainty between investment decisions and induced
hydrogen refueling demand, and proposed a stochastic-robust planning framework for
networked hydrogen-electrical microgrids. Compared with robust optimization, distribu-
tionally robust optimization provides protection against distributional uncertainty while
avoiding excessive conservatism, achieving a better balance between risk and performance.
However, the integration of distributionally robust optimization with decision-dependent
uncertainty under extreme natural disasters is still lacking.
Based on the above, this paper comprehensively considers system operation cost
and environmental scenario load loss cost and proposes a multi-level line hardening
model of the distribution network considering decision-dependent uncertainty. The major
contributions of this paper may be summarized as follows:
(1) A decision-dependent uncertainty (DDU) model for line failure probability based
on disaster intensity is constructed, and a multi-level line-hardening distributionally
robust planning framework is proposed. This model explicitly captures the intrinsic
relationship between hardening levels and failure probability, allowing the uncertainty
set to vary with decision actions. Through the DRO formulation, the framework
jointly considers operational costs and disaster-induced loss, enabling an accurate
characterization of system resilience under extreme weather conditions.
(2) An improved C&CG solution algorithm is developed to address the bilinear and
nested structures introduced by DDU and significantly accelerate convergence. By
incorporating linearization strategies, scenario screening, and convergence-enhancing
techniques, the proposed approach efficiently solves the complex DDU-DRO model
and ensures finite-step convergence.
(3) A system-level numerical study based on typical typhoon wind-speed scenarios is
conducted to validate the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed model.
The results demonstrate that the method substantially reduces worst-case load loss
and enhances sys

sections.title: 2.1 Character of Decision Dependence Uncertainty
sections.text:
The failure probability of the distribution network is affected by multiple factors,
including the design requirements of system components, the intensity of extreme weather,
and the condition of the components during the disaster. Generally, the vulnerability of
power system components reflects the relationship between the failure probability and the
intensity of extreme weather. Based on the vulnerability curve, the relationship between
component failure probability and disaster intensity under different hardening levels and
hardening strategies can be obtained.
Decision-dependent uncertainty (DDU) refers to the uncertainty in which the failure
probability of distribution lines during extreme weather depends on the hardening decision.
Compared with models that ignore DDU, the failure probability of lines in DDU-based
models changes with the hardening decisions, making them more realistic. At the same
disaster scenarios, the failure probability decreases gradually from the un-hardened level
to higher hardening levels. At the same hardening level, the failure probability increases
exponentially with disaster intensity—it rises rapidly after a certain threshold and gradually
approaches one. Therefore, a higher hardening level implies that the line is less likely to
Energies 2025, 18, 6353 4 of 23
fail. Even after hardening, there remains a certain probability of failure under high disaster
intensity, meaning that the line failure probability depends on the hardening decision.
Hence, the multi-level hardening model is a DDU model, where the DDU component is the
failure probability of the line being affected by the hardening decision.
To find the worst-case distribution of failure probabilities, the problem is formulated
to determine the most adverse probability distribution pk of wind speed scenarios in the
uncertain typhoon model. Taking the initial probability pk,0 as the center, an l1-norm or l∞-
norm constraint is adopted to control the deviation of the new probability distribution from
the initial one. The l1-norm constraint reflects the overall deviation or sparsity degree of
probability perturbations, which ensures that the total probability deviation remains within
a reasonable range. The l∞-norm constraint, on the other hand, restricts the maximum
deviation of any single probability from its initial value.
Common distance measures also include KL divergence and JS divergence. Compared
with these two, the l1-norm is linearly tractable and easier to handle in optimization. Hence,
for computational convenience and tractability, the l1-norm is preferred, while the KL and
JS divergences involve nonlinear terms that are more complex to handle.

sections.title: 3.1 Objective Function
sections.text:
In this paper, the distribution network reconfiguration during extreme weather dis-
asters is considered, requiring emergency response and dispatching measures such as
MEG (Mobile Emergency Generator) deployment. A multi-level pre-disaster hardening
model of distribution networks considering decision-dependent uncertainty is proposed to
reflect the influence of typhoon disasters and other extreme weather events on the power
system. The model is applicable not only to typhoon disasters but also to other extreme
weather events such as floods or ice disasters. In addition, for power lines and substations,
the model combines the seismic intensity and failure probability to further expand the
application range. The model mainly applies to short-term, predictable natural disasters of
a single type. The objective function is shown in Equation (4), aiming to minimize the total

sections.title: 4.1 The Customized CCG Algorithm
sections.text:
The number of fault states has a significant impact on the difficulty and computation
time of solving the system. As the number of fault states increases, the combinatorial
problem becomes exponentially complex, which leads to increased computational difficulty
and time consumption. Although a larger set of fault states can provide more comprehen-
sive reference values, in practical applications, deleting some fault states with relatively
small load loss does not affect the final decision results. This optimization strategy helps
the system focus on key fault scenarios, allowing for more efficient decision-making and
hardening deployment, and improving the flexibility and efficiency of the decision process.
Therefore, it is necessary to perform pruning on the fault state set. By screening and optimiz-
ing the reserved fault states with higher impact, this paper proposes a fault-state pruning
method that ensures that the retained fault states cover at least a certain proportion of the
total weighted load loss of the original fault states, thereby improving the computational
efficiency and speed of the decision process.
The steps of the fault-state pruning are as follows:
Step 1: Calculate the weighted load loss δk,g for all fault states, and sort them in
descending order to obtain the set {δr}, r = 1, and set R = 1.
Step 2: Determine whether the following condition is satisfied: ∑R

sections.title: 4.2 Global Sensitivity Analysis Method
sections.text:
Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA) is a statistical framework used to assess how un-
certainty in model inputs propagates to uncertainty in model outputs across the entire
parameter space. Unlike local sensitivity analysis, which examines the derivative of the
output with respect to small perturbations around a nominal point, GSA evaluates the
overall influence of input variables while accounting for their interactions and nonlinear
effects. This enables a more comprehensive understanding of model behavior and the
identification of the most influential parameters that drive system variability.
GSA is particularly useful in complex engineering systems such as power networks,
energy dispatch optimization, and reliability assessment, where model outputs are non-
linear functions of multiple uncertain parameters. The objective is to decompose the total
output variance into portions attributable to each input and their combinations, allowing
Energies 2025, 18, 6353 11 of 23
researchers to quantify the contribution of each uncertainty source to overall model vari-
ance.
The Sobol’ method is a variance-based global sensitivity analysis technique. It relies
on decomposing the model variance into contributions from individual inputs and their
interactions through an Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)-like decomposition. Consider a
mathematical model expressed as:
Y = f (X1, X2, . . . ,Xn), (49)
where Y denotes the model output and Xi (i = 1, 2,. . ., n) are mutually independent input
variables with known probability density functions p(Xi).
The total variance of the output Y is:

The Sobol’ indices provide a clear and interpretable decomposition of model uncer-

4.3. Application of Sobol’ Sensitivity Analysis
In the context of distribution network resilience enhancement, reinforcement decisions
(such as line hardening, component upgrading, or redundancy addition) directly affect the
reliability and performance of the system under extreme conditions. However, the contri-
bution of each reinforcement measure to the overall resilience improvement is not linear,
and multiple reinforcements may interact with each other. To capture these nonlinear
and coupled relationships, the Sobol’ global sensitivity analysis method can be effectively
applied to quantify the contribution of each reinforcement decision to system resilience.
Let the resilience index of the system (e.g., total load restoration ratio or resilience
index value) be represented as a function of reinforcement decisions:
R = f (x1, x2, . . . ,xn), (56)
where R denotes the system resilience evaluation metric, and xi (i = 1, 2,. . ., n) represent
the decision variables corresponding to different reinforcement measures (e.g., line harden-
ing level, substation fortification, distributed generation capacity, etc.). Each xi is treated as
an uncertain variable that reflects the degree or effectiveness of the reinforcement. The goal
is to evaluate how the reinforcement variation in xi affects the variability of the overall
resilience R.
The overall process for applying the Sobol’ method to reinforcement contribution
quantification is as follows:
Step 1: Define input variables. Select reinforcement decision variables x1, x2, . . ., xn
that represent the main hardening or upgrading measures.
Step 2: Establish the resilience evaluation model. Define a resilience index func-
tion R = f (x1, x2, . . ., xn) that maps reinforcement configurations to system performance
(e.g., expected load recovery, outage duration, or fault tolerance).
Step 3: Generate sampling data. Use Monte Carlo or Latin Hypercube Sampling to
generate N random samples of the reinforcement variables within their feasible bounds.
Step 4: Evaluate the model outputs. Compute R(k) = f (x(k)
1 , x(k)
2 , . . ., x(k)
n ) for each
sample k = 1, 2, . . . ,N.
Step 5: Calculate Sobol’ indices. Estimate Si, Sij, and STi using Monte Carlo-based
estimators or the Saltelli sampling scheme.
Step 6: Interpret the results. Rank the reinforcement measures according to Si and STi
values. Identify reinforcements with dominant independent contributions and those with
strong interaction effects.
Reinforcement measures with high Si values are considered the most effective in
directly enhancing system resilience. If (STi − Si) is large, the corresponding reinforcement
has a strong coupling effect, meaning its contribution depends on other reinforcement
actions or system configurations. By analyzing these indices, decision-makers can prioritize
reinforcement strategies with high first order effects for cost-effective resilience improve-
ment, identify synergistic reinforcements that should be implemented jointly, and recognize
redundant or low-impact reinforcements that can be deprioritized.
Thus, Sobol-based sensitivity analysis provides a systematic and quantitative frame-
work for evaluating the contribution and interaction of different reinforcement strategies,
enabling more informed decision-making under limited investment budgets and complex
uncertainty conditions. The flowchart of this paper is shown in Figure 2.

sections.title: 5.1 Parameter Settings
sections.text:
To verify the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed multi-level distributed
robust reinforcement model for distribution networks under uncertainty, a numerical
case study is conducted based on the standard IEEE 33-bus system. Electric vehicle (EV)
charging stations are deployed at buses 14, 30, and distributed generation (DG) units are
installed at buses 14, 21, and 24. Five tie lines are configured between buses 8–21, 9–15,
12–22, 18–33, and 25–29. The virtual line represents a branch that is disconnected under
normal operating conditions. The voltage magnitude limits of all nodes are set within
0.95–1.05 p.u.
In this study, the reinforcement measures are implemented in the form of pole tower
strengthening and cable management. Different material strengths are adopted for pole
reinforcement, while the cable enhancement is realized through cross-sectional upgrad-
ing. Three reinforcement cost levels are considered, corresponding to Level 1, Level 2,
and Level 3, with costs of CNY 200,000, CNY 300,000, and CNY 500,000, respectively.
The wind-speed data are shown in the following figure. In this study, the pruning ratio
cut for scenario reduction is set to 0.95. The hardening coefficients correspond to the three
reinforcement levels, with Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 assigned coefficients of two, four,
and six, respectively.
Extreme weather events such as typhoons are assumed to cause wide-area failures
within the system. The typhoon coverage is simulated from 10:00 a.m. and lasts for
several hours. Based on historical typhoon path and wind speed data, three representative
wind-speed scenarios are generated, each corresponding to different disaster intensities.
The wind speed scenarios are sampled using a large dataset of recorded typhoon data,
and their probabilistic distributions are constructed via Monte Carlo simulation to ensure
the diversity and representativeness of the scenarios.The wind-speed information is shown
in Figure 3.
In each wind-speed scenario, six fault states are generated according to the probabilistic
distribution of component failures. The reduction ratio of the fault states is determined
Energies 2025, 18, 6353 14 of 23
through scenario pruning, and the final number of representative fault states is retained for
further analysis.
Figure 3. The wind scenarios of extreme weather disaster.

sections.title: 5.2 Planning Schemes Comparison
sections.text:
To better demonstrate the advantages of the proposed model, five planning schemes
are designed for comparison. In all cases, the total reinforcement budget is set to CNY
1.2 million. In these scenarios, the system includes 50 electric vehicles (EVs) willing to
participate in grid interaction, divided into five groups, each containing 10 EVs. Each EV
has a rated discharging power of 2 kW and a rated battery capacity of 10 kWh.
During extreme natural disasters, the willingness of EV users to participate in grid
interaction significantly decreases. EVs possess a high degree of mobility and flexibility,
and their participation in vehicle-to-grid (V2G) operations can be encouraged through
governmental incentives or subsidies. It is worth noting that when a fault occurs in the
distribution network, both grid-charging and grid-discharging modes of EVs are possible.
If the fault causes a loss of power supply, EVs will automatically switch to the discharging
mode to support the grid.
This study focuses on voluntary participation of EVs in grid regulation. To avoid
possible over-discharge and to reduce battery degradation, the SOC (state of charge) of each
EV is constrained within a safe operating range during disaster periods. The upper and
lower limits of SOC are set according to the operational requirements, and the minimum
SOC is allowed to drop to the lower limit during the recovery phase. In the studied
system, there is one MEG (mobile emergency generator) station located at node 11. The
configuration of the five planning schemes is summarized in Table 1.
